To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have designed a GTPase and its cognate GEF to interact in a manner that is orthogonal to all other known cellular GTPase/GEF interactions.

we have computationally redesigned a GTPase/GEF protein pair to be orthogonal to the endogenous GEFs of the cell and that we have used this pair to engineer orthogonal signaling pathways in living cells.

we have computationally designed a GTPase/GEF protein pair with an affinity for each other of 10–100 times greater than for any other GTPase/ GEF pair, and have demonstrated that this pair functions in living cells with no interference or cross-talk with endogenous cellular signaling pathways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
engineering protein–protein interactions to create novel signaling pathways in mammalian cells.
the rational design and implementation of orthogonal protein interactions in living cells.
the development of new computational and experimental approaches to the design and construction of protein–protein interactions and protein signaling pathways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“orthogonal” protein interactions have been engineered and that they can be used to build new signaling pathways in cells.
“the engineered GEF/GTPase pair can function in the presence of the native GEF/GTPases without interfering with their normal cellular function” (1).
the study demonstrates the successful computational design of orthogonal signaling interactions in cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we designed a new GTPase/GEF pair that is functionally equivalent to the natural pair but is completely orthogonal in its behavior to the natural pair in living cells.
we have developed a generalizable method to computationally redesign protein interactions that can be used for the design of orthogonal protein interactions in vivo.
we have designed a protein–protein interaction that can be added to cells without interfering with the endogenous protein–protein interactions that are already present.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it is indeed possible to design protein interactions that are orthogonal to their cellular environment, and that the design process can be guided by computational methods that take the cellular context into account.

the design of an orthogonal signaling pathway requires the design of orthogonal interactions, and this can be achieved computationally by the use of a scoring function that is based on a structural description of the interaction.
the design of orthogonal signaling pathways is possible and that the design of such orthogonal interactions can be achieved through a combination of rational design and computational modeling.
